newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Central bank uncertainty hits gold.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Central bank uncertainty hits gold.

text.p: The prospect that European central banks will sell more gold as Europe heads for a union of its monetary system is weighing on the gold price, Rothschild Australia Ltd managing director Richard Lee said on Wednesday.
"There is concern that the volume of sales coming out of that sector will increase as a result of the movement toward the European monetary union," Lee told Reuters in an interview.
"The principal negative factor affecting sentiment is that," Lee said.
Gold has taken a hammering since the start of the year and currently hovers around three year lows at about US$346 an ounce.

Beyond any potential further central bank disposal of gold, the gold market was sound fundamentally, with significant amounts of metal required annually from stockpiles to match up supply and demand, Lee said.
Demand for gold has been in persistent deficits since 1988 as a direct result of the needs of jewellery and other metal fabricators outpacing supplies mined each year, he said.
"Demand for gold is still very strong," he said. "If one could ignore the stocks of gold held by central banks, I think it would be a very bullish outlook."
Analysts estimate about 35,000 tonnes of gold are held by central banks worldwide.

Lee said the move to a single currency among West European nations will foster central bank gold sales, but reserved judgement on whether it would mean the volume of gold leaving the bank vaults each year would change.
"It is difficult to get a fix on whether it will significantly change the volume of sales," he said.
Europe's central banks traditionally hold more gold than other central banks, therefore it is logical these banks would be reducing their reserves, he said.
European central banks were under pressure to comply with European monetary requirements, Lee said.
"An easy way to meet those requirement is to sell an asset that's undervalued on your balance sheet," he said.
Still, the market reaction to the possibility of fresh gold sales has been overstated somewhat, Lee said.
"They will be sellers of gold and they have been sellers of gold for several years ... I just don't see that it's in the interest of central banks to dump gold," he said.
